newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries recover late to end slightly lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries recover late to end slightly lower.

text.p: Aided by a surge in the dollar, U.S. Treasuries recovered Monday afternoon to close a touch lower.
The 30-year bond ended the day at 101-27/32, down 1/32 from Friday. Its yield was unchanged at 6.36 percent.
"The (positive) tone that we ended November on is still in place," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston Corp. "Longs are not looking to take profits."
Treasuries had been depressed most of the session, mostly on stronger than expected economic news early in the session.
For starters, news reports said consumers shopped until they dropped over the Thanksgiving weekend, suggesting the holiday shopping season could be the strongest in many years.

Later in the morning, the market was hit with a double whammy of strong data: a rise in the overall National Association of Purchasing Management index in November to 52.7 from 50.2 in October and a surprising 1.8 percent jump in construction spending in October.
The market had anticipated a NAPM number in the 50 to 51 range, while construction spending was expected to fall about 1.0 percent.

Plus, the run-up Friday -- primarily on technical factors related to month-end book-squaring -- was said to have been excessive, and spawned a retreat on Monday, pushing the long-bond down as much as 14/32 early in the session.
"It was a natural correction," said a head trader at a large U.S. bank. "The run-up Friday was overdone. There was some selling, taking back what we picked up Friday in a thin market."
But, as has been the case in recent months, the selloff could not be sustained.
Analysts said a rise in the dollar helped rescue Treasuries from their lows. The dollar jumped to 1.5590 German marks -- a 23-month high -- before falling back to 1.5555 late in the session.
"The dollar's continued strength has been something to watch," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "It helped put a floor where (Treasury) prices could go today.
"Comments by European officials jawboning the dollar higher had a ripple effect in our market," he said.
"The market was listless most of the day and people were looking for direction. The (dollar's) move helped it out," added Alexy.
Alexy noted that the dollar's rise should give Treasuries a bid during the night in overseas trading.
Also helping Treasuries rally late in the session was the realization the NAPM report wasn't all that bad, since the prices index fell to 45.9 in November from 47.1 in October.
"The fact that it remained below 50 and moved lower from the prior month helped soften the blow," Flanagan said, noting that the other NAPM components were on the robust side.
The two-year note ended 100-1/32, down 1/32, to yield 5.61 percent. The 10-year note was down 3/32 at 103-7/32 to yield 6.06 percent.

But while coupons ended lower, bills put in a strong performance -- especially at the front end. The year-bill was at 5.11 percent, up two basis points from Friday. The six-month bill was unchanged at 5.04 percent, but the three-month bill was down six basis points at 4.94 percent.
"Dealers were buying in anticipation of reinvestment demand," said Richard Schwarz, a senior bill trader at Zions First National Bank, noting the lack of professional players.
While not a huge factor, some players also said the market was encouraged by early signals on the Boskin report's findings on the overstatement of the consumer price index.
Market participants don't expect the festive mood to dissipate in the near future, and expect bonds to trade within narrow ranges until Friday's November employment report.
Tuesday, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi/Schroder Wertheim weekly chain store sales report, the October leading indicators index and Redbook retail sales data are due.
Schwarz explained that with numerous cash management bills matururing in the next couple weeks, dealers expect much of that reinvestment money going into paper 30 to 90 days.
Monday, the Treasury sold $28 billion three- and six-month bills at average discount rates of 4.98 percent and 5.04 percent, respectively.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
